references.text: The Mosaic law commanded that lepers should cry out, "unclean, unclean," and keep their distance from other people. The ten lepers in Luke 17:12 who stood far away followed this command from Leviticus 13:45-46.
In Numbers 5:2-3 it is commanded that lepers be sent outside the camp so as not to make it unclean. This explains why the ten lepers in Luke kept their distance and stood far away from Jesus.

Gehazi was struck with Naaman's leprosy in 2 Kings 5:27, which shows that leprosy was seen as a serious condition linked to God's judgment, making the healing of the ten lepers in Luke even more remarkable.

The account of Naaman the leper in 2 Kings 5:1-14 is an important background for the story of the ten lepers. Jesus himself referred to Naaman in Luke 4:27, and both stories concern lepers who are healed and include a connection to Samaritans/Gentiles.
Leviticus 14:2-3 describes the procedure for cleansing lepers, which Jesus refers to in Luke 17:14 when he tells the ten lepers to show themselves to the priests.
In Luke 5:12-13 Jesus heals a leper, an earlier account of Jesus' power over leprosy that parallels the healing of the ten lepers in chapter 17.
In Matthew 8:2-3 a leper comes to Jesus and is healed, showing Jesus' willingness and ability to heal lepers, parallel to the account in Luke 17:12.

In Luke 4:27 Jesus notes that there were many lepers in Israel during the time of the prophet Elisha, but only Naaman the Syrian was cleansed. This theme of an outsider receiving grace is repeated when in Luke 17:16 it is the Samaritan – the foreigner – who returns to give thanks.
